outcomes: Says what each of the first ten moves of the Queen's Gambit Declined prepares (the pressure on d5, the pin on f6, the support for d4, castling) and checks it by counting attackers and defenders

Avoids the Elephant Trap as White by checking what Black's bishop move threatens after the knight leaves c3, and knows that different move orders can reach the same position

line.say: White takes space and opens the way for the queen and bishop.

steps.caption: Moves four. White's bishop looks at the knight that defends d5; Black's reply decides how much that matters.

After ...Be7 the bishop defends the knight on f6.

steps.caption: Move five. White supports the centre and opens the bishop on f1; Black castles.

line.say: The pawn supports d4 and opens the diagonal of the bishop on f1.
Black's king goes to safety and a rook comes towards the centre.

claims.statement: The pawn on e3 supports the pawn on d4.
After e3 the bishop on f1 sees e2 and d3.

steps.text: **What strong players chose** (results, not evaluations). Source: our masters data, 329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more. In the position after five moves each, 151 games continue: the knight move to f3 in 108 (White won 25, 65 were drawn, Black won 18), the queen move to c2 in 26 and a rook move to c1 in 17. Counts are small; results also reflect who played.

**Black's problem piece.** Black's pawns on d5 and e6 stand on light squares, the same colour as the bishop on c8. [I] A bishop shut in by its own pawns is called a bad bishop. Here it has a single move, to d7. Most of Black's early plans in this opening are ways to free it. The next board counts the pawns and the moves.
steps.chapter: Black's bad bishop and three ways out

steps.caption: Black to move after 6.Nf3. Count Black's pawns by square colour, then count the moves of the bishop on c8.

claims.statement: Black has 5 pawns on light squares and 3 on dark squares.
The bishop on c8 has exactly one legal move.

steps.text: **Three ways to free the bishop** [I]. One: trade the knight and a pair of pieces so the bishop gets room (the Lasker idea). Two: play ...b6 and put the bishop on b7 (the Tartakower set-up). Three: take on c4 and bring the bishop out later; you met that in the previous lesson. The names are the usual ones [R]. The next boards show the first two.

steps.caption: The Lasker idea, part one: a trade of minor pieces. Black asks the bishop on g5 a question, then swings the knight out.

line.say: White develops: the knight attacks e5 and g5.
Black asks the bishop on g5 to decide.
The bishop keeps the pin on f6.
The knight leaps out. If it is taken, the d5 pawn recaptures.
White trades the pinning bishop before it is lost.
Black recaptures, and one pair of minor pieces is gone.

claims.statement: The knight on f3 attacks e5 and g5.
The pawn on h6 attacks g5.
The bishop on h4 attacks f6.
The knight on e4 attacks c3 and f2.
At depth 16 the position is level or slightly better for White, about a third of a pawn at most.

steps.caption: The Lasker idea, part two: more trades. With fewer pieces each of Black's remaining pieces gets more squares, and the bishop on c8 needs squares. Black supports d5, then trades the second pair of knights.

line.say: The rook goes to the c-file.
Black supports d5 and prepares to give up the centre pawn.
The bishop clears f1 for castling and still covers c4.
Black trades the second pair.
White recaptures with the rook.

claims.statement: The rook on c1 stands on the open c-file.
The pawn on c6 defends d5.
After Be2 the square f1 is empty.

steps.caption: Then the capture on c4. Black takes the pawn, White regains it, the last knight comes out and White castles.

line.say: Black takes the pawn. The d5 pawn has left; the bishop's partner is gone.
White regains the pawn.
The last knight comes out; ...e5 or ...b6 will free the bishop.
White castles; the position is balanced.

claims.statement: After ...dxc4 the square d5 is empty.
At depth 16 the final position is balanced: White is ahead by at most about a third of a pawn.

steps.caption: The Tartakower set-up. Black frees the bishop in a different way: a pawn move that gives it two new squares.

line.say: The pawn move opens b7 and a6 for the bishop.
The bishop eyes h7 and backs up the c4 pawn that presses on d5.
The bishop reaches the long diagonal, behind its own pawn on d5 for now.
White castles; both kings are safe.
The last minor piece comes out and defends f6.
[I] The queen supports the bishop on d3 and prepares to put the rooks on the open files.

claims.statement: After ...b6 the bishop on c8 has three legal moves (b7, a6, d7).
The bishop on d3 attacks h7.
The bishop on b7 sees c6 and its own pawn on d5.
After castling the white king is on the kingside.
The knight on d7 defends f6.
At depth 16 the position is balanced: within about half a pawn of level.

steps.caption: White can release the tension on d5. Black to move: one recapture follows the plan and the other is worse by at least 0.15 pawn [V], because the e-pawn recapture leaves the c8 bishop shut in a little longer [I]. Then step through the trades.

line.say: Recapturing with the knight keeps the pawn structure healthy and aims at trades.
White trades the bishop that was pinning.
Black recaptures.
White trades the knights.
Black retakes with the e-pawn. This is an exchange structure like Carlsbad, but with Black's pawn still on c7.

claims.statement: At depth 16 Nxd5 is the engine's first choice here.
Recapturing with the e-pawn is worse than the best move by at least 0.15 pawn.
After the trades the c-file is half-open for White and the e-file for Black.
At depth 16 the position is level.

steps.text: **Which to choose? [H]** The Lasker plan trades pieces and simplifies; the Tartakower plan keeps more pieces and the long diagonal. [H] A player who likes quiet positions may prefer the first, a player who likes more pieces the second. Our masters data: of 581 games reaching the position after the bishop retreat to h4, Black played the pawn move b6 in 274, the knight jump to e4 in 173 and the knight move to d7 in 124.

steps.title: Is the knight leap ready?
steps.prompt: In all three positions Black considers ...Ne4. Predict for each whether it is within 0.4 pawn of the engine's best move, then check. The second differs from the first in one feature: Black's d-pawn stands on d6 instead of d5. The third adds two quiet moves.

steps.caption: Why the second position fails: a trade on e4 needs a recapture, and with the pawn on d6 nothing recaptures. Step through what happens when Black leaps without one.

Black recaptures.

steps.text: **White's menu after castling.** [I] Nf3 develops and prepares to castle. Rc1 puts a rook on the file where the c-pawn will leave. The queen move to c2 supports the e-pawn and the bishop on d3. Which is best depends on what Black does next. Our data: in 345 games with the bishop on h4 and Black's knight on d7, White played the rook move to c1 in 181, the queen move to c2 in 104 and the bishop move to e2 in 22.

steps.text: **Mixed tests.** Four positions follow with no hints about the theme. Before each move ask the checking questions: what did the opponent's last move attack, how often is the key square attacked and defended, and which pawn has left which square? One of the four may have more than one good answer.

**Recap.**
- Each early move changes how often d5 is attacked and defended.
- The pin on f6 is met by the bishop to e7 and, later, by the pawn question.
- Black's bishop on c8 is the problem piece: one move, shut in by its own light pawns.
- Three exits: trade pieces (Lasker), pawn to b6 (Tartakower), capture on c4.
- The knight leap needs a recapture on e4 and a safe bishop on e7.
- Different move orders can reach one position; check which trades each allows.

**Self-check list for your teach-back.** Did you name what at least four early moves prepare? Did you say why the bishop on c8 is the problem piece, and name two ways out? Did you say when the knight leap is safe and when it loses a piece? Did you give a move-order example a beginner could set up? Fix any gap before the final line.
